explain.say: In 1556 a boy of thirteen became Mughal emperor after his father fell down a library staircase. Half a century later Akbar ruled most of northern India, from Kabul to Bengal. Look at the timeline of how he built and held that empire.

explain.say: How do you hold such an empire? See the network. Akbar ranked his officers as mansabdars, from mansab, rank. Each rank set a salary and the number of cavalry to supply. Revenue came from peasants through local landholders called zamindars. Why would ranks and pay set by the emperor keep nobles loyal?

Look at 1562 and 1564. Akbar made marriage alliances with Rajput kings, who became top commanders, and abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, in 1564. Most of his subjects were Hindu. Why might a ruler choose partnership over force?

explain.say: Look at the map: Agra, Lahore, and the frontier at Kabul. Near Agra he built Fatehpur Sikri, where from 1575 his House of Worship hosted Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars. His ideal was sulh-i kul, peace with all. Can you think of a modern country that uses a similar idea?

See the debate. His court historian Abul Fazl praised a wise ruler; the scholar Badauni secretly wrote that Akbar had strayed from Islam. Historians read both. Brilliant work. Exam tip: when you use a court history, ask who paid the writer.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Two insiders, two very different Akbars.

faq.q: Why is Akbar called the Great?
faq.a: Because he expanded the Mughal Empire across most of northern and central India, built a lasting administration with the mansabdari and revenue systems, and pursued a policy of tolerance, sulh-i kul, towards his diverse subjects.
Akbar's ranking system for officials and nobles. Each mansabdar held a numbered rank that fixed his pay and the cavalry he must provide; ranks were set by the emperor and were not hereditary.

faq.q: Why did Akbar ally with the Rajputs?
faq.a: Rajput kings had strong armies and local authority. By marriage alliances, high ranks and respect for their autonomy, Akbar turned many from rivals into partners, starting with Amber in 1562. He also abolished the jizya in 1564.
asks: When did Akbar abolish the jizya?

faq.a: Sulh-i kul, peace with all: equal treatment of religions, debates in the Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship, at Fatehpur Sikri from 1575, and an end to taxes on non-Muslims. A small devotional circle around him, the Din-i Ilahi, is debated by historians.

faq.q: Who were Abul Fazl and Badauni?
faq.a: Two writers at Akbar's court. Abul Fazl wrote the official Akbarnama praising the emperor; Abd al-Qadir Badauni wrote a private chronicle criticising Akbar's religious experiments. Together they show competing views.

facts: Akbar became emperor in 1556 at the age of 13.
Fatehpur Sikri was built from 1571 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
